quote: It hardly surprised Will that the train ticket to Bloodgrove bore a bloody fingerprint. Last night, when doubts about his plan had troubled him, he had lifted the card to his mouth, cautiously put out his tongue, and licked the stain. People said there were mages in Bloodgrove who could read any person's identity from only a few drops of blood.

Just as he reached for the door, it swung open, and from the darkness of the carriage a gaunt face stared back at him, its cheeks hollow and sunken. The cap of a conductor's livery sat upon strawy hair.

Though he was the last person entitled to doubt magic, he still found blood-magic difficult to believe in. It sounded suspiciously like propaganda and fairy tales, much like all the other horrors people told one another about mysterious Bloodgrove. Even so, he felt a flicker of disappointment when the conductor tore the ticket and handed back the unstained remainder.

A shadow moved through the train's cloud of steam, striding swiftly across the platform, one hand pulling a hat low over his face. Smoke caught in the long tails of a coat, and a walking stick flashed in the weak sunlight. The next moment, the passenger had vanished.

But how could he, only twenty-six, have borne the weight of those expectations? Even now, he could see the construction site at night, hear the echo of impatient voices asking how much longer it would take—and feel the desperation with which he had reached for the knife and called upon his magic.
Even now, he thought he could taste salt on his tongue. Goosebumps crawled over his arms. His lover had suddenly been standing before him with the queen's cousin, the guards' rifles trained on Will.
To avoid a scandal and the charges that would follow, he fled the city.

It is time for your light to illuminate Bloodgrove and usher in a new age. My house has been in my family's keeping for centuries, and now that I am head of it, I wish my vision to shape these ancient walls as well.
Tear down what has gathered dust. Cast aside what holds no value in a new world. You have free rein.
“He made an exception for me.” She smiled, but it did nothing to soften her face. “Our King is exceedingly well disposed toward my family.”

His walking stick struck the floor with every step until, in one fluid motion, he lifted it and caught it at the center. Only now did Will see the silver handle—a wolf's head with its jaws stretched wide.
Slowly, his gaze traveled along the gentleman's arm, clad in a perfectly tailored, if unfashionable, suit, and upward to the sharp features of a man around Will's own age.
“That is Mr. Eric Arcos, the Red Ambassador,” Duchess Wilkinson murmured.

A bird lay before him with its wings spread wide, their pitch-black feathers hanging over the rim of the plate and revealing a plucked, roasted body. The beets inside its head shimmered purple in the light of the table lamp and the last echo of sunset.
“You aren't eating?” he asked, but the lady shook her head.
Will swallowed his disappointment. His wish had been selfish. He wanted another glimpse of that handsome face, wanted to study the contrasts between the pale skin, light eyes, and dark hair.

It was as though someone had gathered every cathedral in the world, hurled them against the slope, and left them to tower over one another in endless cascades of spires and pointed arches, gables and eaves, stone pennants and gargoyles.

What a name for a city in which one feared slicing open a hand with a single careless movement. A perversion of an idyllic grove nestled between babbling brooks and summer lindens—distorted and blackened. Perhaps that was where the rumors of curses and dark magic came from, for the city looked as though an evil mage had built it.

No, it could not be an escape when everything in his body was screaming at him to leave this place. It would have been an escape if he had torn up the letter and the bloody ticket, burned them in a fireplace, and boarded a train heading south. But this, he told himself as his heart hammered, was continuing the fight for his dream.

The lady's maid stepped back, and the light brushed the duchess's face—or the place where her face ought to have been. A steel mask, wrought as delicately as the tracery adorning Bloodgrove's buildings, encased her head.

“He shares with us his dream of sunrise over the sea, amid pink spray and white clouds. Mr. Frank does not strive for practicality or commercial appeal, but rather to make the visitor pause and marvel when the heart itself whispers ‘home’. Those are grand words, Mr. Frank.”
“Good. All of this is my father's work, but I am now the head of this family, and I want to burn his rot and decay from these walls. Replace it with ‘pink spray and white clouds,’ should you wish.”
“Bloodgrove is a swamp. It is time we remind its people of that and bring the future even to our forgotten corner of the world. Break the old curses and bring the world to us.”
It all sounded suspiciously like the very thing from which he had fled, and for a moment panic threatened to drive its blade into his heart. He swiftly forced it down.
“And Mr. Frank—I strongly advise you not to leave the house after dark.”
“You should close the curtains. You already look like one of the moon children.”

It struck like lightning and lingered, coursing through his torso and lower body. Groaning, he put a hand to his stomach and froze. His belly arched like a dome of taut, pale skin, large, round, and hard.
But he saw it clearly in the moonlight; saw something shifting there. He felt it glide beneath the skin like a lindworm moving under the surface of a lake.
“Isn't it wonderful, my dearest?” a voice whispered from the darkness. It sounded like the roaring sea in a storm.

“Not yet. The time has not yet come. My beautiful one, adieu,” the voice whispered, suddenly close beside him, and then it was gone. As though it had taken the storm with it, the shadows stilled and made room for the peace of night.

Will dared to exhale, but his breath caught. Something still pressed upward against his lungs, his diaphragm, his belly. With a twitch, the worm stirred again, growing larger, making his stomach swell further until his skin was stretched to the point of tearing.

Even the bath the servants had drawn for him had failed to rinse away the clammy feeling the dream had left behind. The echo of foreign organs remained. Will put his hand to his heart and listened to its steady rhythm, reassuring himself that no second heartbeat answered.

But what made him stare were the heavy chains hanging everywhere from the ceiling, sometimes a pair, sometimes two, each ending in iron manacles. Beneath them, the parquet was darkened with large, reddish-brown stains.
Slowly, the butler stepped onto the stained wood. “The old master succumbed to the bloodlust.”

He forced his mind to remain with the familiar and locked magic and dreams inside a forgotten chamber in his chest. He would finish what he had lost in the queen's cousin's ballroom, facing whatever it takes.
“She had two sisters. One died with a dead child in her womb. The other took her own life.”
“Who is the fourth child?” he finally managed as he rose again.

“Mr. Frank, you are an outsider. You do things differently from the way they are done here. You have no respect for this family or for the power of this house. Until Her Grace takes personal charge of the work, that responsibility falls to me.”
And the butler obeyed. The tradespeople remained cautious, but they were no longer afraid. It was Will himself they seemed to distrust.

A long, slender neck held a heart-shaped face with eyes the color of the sea. She was raw and beautiful, with unruly brows, severe lips, and sharp collarbones above soft, full breasts. The milky light traced her silhouette against the dark corridor behind her, her black mane merging with the shadows as though the ghost he had sensed these past few days had taken the shape of a woman.
Elodie looked up with a lazy smile. “Money is not the price.”
“Not yet. Do not leave the house. In here, I am the most dangerous thing you are likely to find.” She smiled innocently.

“You look rather like a moon child yourself. My mother used to tell us stories of creatures with hair as white as cobwebs, skin as white as bone, eyes as white as pearls, and teeth as white as the crescent moon.”
“Good. Otherwise I would have to worry that you might seduce me into walking into the sea and drowning before I ever reached your kingdom on the moon.”

“You ask as though you were a magician who could conjure anything.” Elodie reached for the next sample book, and only then did he notice the discreet bandages around her forearms. He was ashamed he had overlooked them until now, when they seemed so plainly visible: beige against her cream-colored skin.

“A pity.” She beamed at him, her grey eyes sparkling. “I need something magical. The parlor and the ballroom should enchant my guests; draw them in like moths to a flame. Remind them of everything they are missing beyond this city. And who knows? Perhaps something may even change.”

Will followed more slowly, first down the stairs and then across the broad atrium with its black-and-white tiles, until his hand closed around the door handle. The bolt had not been drawn, and Hedgefort was nowhere in sight. It felt forbidden, as though he were a child defying his tutors, which was utterly ridiculous.
Saint moved closer still, even rising onto his toes, though the mischief in his expression had given way to a sharper look as he studied Will's eyes.
“I would not go down there if I were you. Monsters hunt in those streets.”

“Elodie? Elodie Ormonde? She is your patron?” Mr. Arcos's perfect, courteous expression slipped, revealing a flash of genuine surprise—something, Will was certain, that was rarely seen. At the same time, he knew he had made a mistake.
Mr. Arcos smiled slowly, and Will shivered. “Of course. We were childhood friends.”

“Magic is not forbidden here in Bloodgrove. Those who drink too much blood and surrender to the frenzy are banished to the southern districts, where they rob, pillage, and kill. I would advise you not to enter those areas unarmed, even in daylight.”

The ambassador ran a gloved hand through his hair, revealing scattered silver strands among the raven black. “My first grey appeared when I was fourteen.” His hair was cut in a way to conceal it at first glance, and the silver showed only when he swept it to the other side.
“After sunset?”
My carriage will await you outside the Ormonde residence at seven o'clock.

The opera began, telling the dramatic story of a golden city's fall, and Will slowly came to understand Mr. Arcos's intentions. He almost laughed at the way the ambassador had put him on display and made a mockery of him, and how naïvely Will had walked straight into the trap. He ignored the sharp sting of disappointment.

They were all pale, or—where their complexions did not allow for pallor—an unhealthy grey. Their clothing was fastened so tightly to the throat that the collars seemed to strangle them. More than one hand stroked hungrily over the fabric of Will's suit, and he forced himself not to recoil.

“We all know the steep price one must pay for a ticket, but it was important to me that this rare visitor be brought to our city,” he continued. “Allow me to introduce Mr. William Frank. My…” He looked at Will expectantly.
So Will gave them his most charming smile. “Interior designer.”

Oh, so it had been a game after all. Only Will had never been its target—Elodie had. Now he remembered the surprise on Arcos's face when her name had slipped his lips, and the sudden change in his demeanor. Ambassador Eric Arcos had never been interested in him, only in the duchess, and she was furious.

“Because you were meant to be my grand reveal. I paid for your ticket. I am housing you. I am going to present a project the entire city will speak of. I will break the curse and open our city to the world.”

“How much do you know about our city?” she paused. “Our King has withdrawn from public life, and the Red Hand oversees the daily affairs of Bloodgrove as his representative. He is the most powerful man in the city.”

But Elodie was faster. She drew the blood from her palm like an illusionist pulling a scarf from his sleeve, then flung it toward the woman. In midair, it formed a blade and buried itself in her skull. The body crumpled to the ground with a dull thud.
“That was a vampire?” He glanced over his shoulder, but in that moment the darkness came alive. Figures rushed from the alleys and descended upon the motionless body.
Elodie had barely caught her breath before she stormed toward Eric Arcos. “You have some nerve showing your face here!”
Deep in his bones, Will knew Elodie had done the right thing, that the woman had been more than a desperate beggar. He could still see the madness in her eyes.
“What are you doing?” he asked as the ambassador raised the blood to his lips and licked it away.

“Because this is the only language we know. We have hated each other since childhood. We will fight until one of us is in the grave, and even then, the other will try to build a larger mausoleum beside it.”

“I chose that opera because, as a child in Bloodgrove, it was where I first heard of the Capitol—the magical golden city beyond the mountains, ruled by a powerful queen. To a poor child like me, it was an unreachable place, but I wanted to fight for the chance to travel there one day.”
“But the night has only just begun,” Mr. Arcos replied without turning, and vanished into the dark. Will caught one last glimpse of him as he drew a concealed blade from his walking stick.

In the morning, he had felt filthy because he had dreamed of lust and longing rather than horror at a woman's death. Perhaps a nightmare would have been easier, though he had no wish to carry another worm inside him.
“What would they say? Every house of rank has secrets like these. But most have the decency to indulge them in tiled rooms.”
“I am receiving guests tomorrow. I advise you to remain in your room.” Something in her usual warmth fell away.
He knew Elodie had wanted to keep him hidden, but he would be careful. Magic sang to him, familiar as his mother's voice and distant as if from a grave.
Pride will be their downfall, and indolence their end. Again and again, they underestimate us. They think we are content to endure the same monsters that tormented our parents!
Elodie seized one of his arms and forced it straight. “By blood! Accept my offering!”

“Serve the one who gives you life!” the duchess cried. She let the dagger fall, dipped one finger into the blood now pouring from the wound, and began to write in the air. Glowing red, it remained suspended before her. Words and symbols formed, pulsing with a heartbeat of their own.

The monster found its feet and rose to its full, immense height. It stood more than two meters tall, with long arms, matted fur, and skin stretched taut over its ribs and shoulders. Half man, half wolf.
Magic held him down, and his body swayed gently with the melody. But then something began to pound inside his chest. A second heartbeat—one that did not match the rhythm of the invocation.

“Enough!” His voice thundered through the room, and everything stopped. The air froze. Ice crystals glittered in the candlelight. He had no idea what he was doing; the words shaped themselves on his lips. Something more natural than his heartbeat spoke through him.
Will no longer felt like himself as he stepped closer, until Elodie's skirts brushed his legs. His body was only a small fragment of what he was, no more than a ship, while his soul was the sea.

Magic spoke to magic. Will knew that his power was a sister to what Elodie had called forth. Perhaps not a sister—perhaps a lover, an old companion recognizing the touch with which they had once danced.

“The god of the Winter Sea.” His voice was still not his own. Neither was the searching hand driven by magic as it moved along the tender skin of her thigh. Elodie sighed, while behind her the monster crushed the vampire's skull between its teeth. The guests hummed in their trance.

With a strangled cry, he forced the magic back and pressed his soul once more into the inadequate shape of his body. He stumbled away as panic overwhelmed him. The fear had been there all along, but whatever had taken control of him had pushed it aside. Now he saw the entire grotesque scene and fled.
“Albatross. God of the Winter Sea.” Will did not know how the words had found their way to his lips, yet he felt their truth.

“Blood.” Elodie searched his face as though she expected to find recognition there. “A castle made of flesh and bodies without skin. Black night pulsing with red veins. Eyes watching me from everywhere, like stars across the heavens.”

“I dream of albatrosses and salted honey.” He didn't dare to say more. Perhaps she knew what he meant. Even so, he hoped to see some spark of recognition in her, while at the same time fearing her disgust.

“I cannot tell you whether you should trust your dreams. In Bloodgrove, they play cruel tricks. Plenty of wine before bed helps.” Her fingers traced the rim of her cup as the first hint of pink slowly reached the narrow courtyard alley.

“Nothing else happened, and thanks to your help, we were able to stabilize the ritual. Soon we will know whether it succeeded. But already the city will be talking about an eighth contender in the race for the Red Hand. And what is a blood incantation without a few deaths?”
“Perhaps you truly are not some great sorcerer,” Elodie continued, tilting her head as she studied him. “And yet… What was that last night? Who spoke through you?”

“You as a woman and you as a mage are inseparable. Last night, I could not tell which tempted me more.” His voice was rough, and he had forgotten why he had stepped so close. She took control with effortless ease.
“It is already improper for an unmarried woman such as myself to share her home with a young man like you,” she said coolly. “We should not repeat a meeting like this.”

A temple, high and airy, spreading wide as the crown of a tree. Chandeliers floated overhead like golden clouds, lit by the setting sun. This ballroom was not the black of the witching hour, but the azure of dusk, when the veil between the faerie realm and their own grew thin, and maidens danced with fauns and young men with elves until the soles of their shoes wore through.

“Have you lost your mind, setting a chimera on me during a council session?” Mr. Arcos shouted. Only then did Will notice the long cuts across his face, the bandaged hand, and the spatters of blood reaching into his hair.
You spend blood as though you have nothing to lose! You paid the blood toll to bring in a damned interior designer. For what? So you can host prettier balls?
“Because you want to become the next Red Hand,” Mr. Arcos said, stunned. “Still.”

“Do not speak to me of loss while you stand here taking away everything I have fought for!” Something shifted in her expression. Her brows drew together, and Will might almost have called it concern as she studied the cuts on Mr. Arcos's face. “You should have those wounds tended to.”

“What do you want with him? Why did you not rent him rooms like any normal person?” he asked with sudden intensity, and Will understood something all at once: Mr. Arcos had never been interested in him.
“You are sleeping with him.” This time, Mr. Arcos took the time to study Will more closely. “He looks as though he has only just climbed out of bed—and thoroughly satisfied.” His eyes narrowed.
Elodie let her cool gaze travel over Arcos. “It is time for you to leave, before I find enough of your blood on my floor to force you out.”

“Keep me out of your rivalry,” he said calmly. “I am beginning to understand that the rules of your games are beyond me, and that my safety is not among them. I am your employee, someone you pay to do a job, and that job ends at the door to this ballroom.”
“Being manipulated, bringing monsters back to life, and gaining a reputation as your lover were not part of our agreement.”
While dressing for the evening, he had decided to trust Elodie. Behind that pretty face, gears were always turning and pieces of a mosaic falling into place, forming a picture only she could see.
“A lack of courage… It prevents strangers from cutting us and stealing our blood.”
The moment her arms closed around him, she exploded.
“He looks even more beautiful in red!”

Oh, his anger was cold. If he opened his mouth now, a winter storm would ride his tongue and blow ice crystals into their sparkling wine glasses until their breath failed and their fingers turned first pale, then blue. Sixteen people frozen in the midst of their laughter.

Still, he followed her, and the moment the washroom door closed behind them, he spun around and wrapped his fingers around her throat. Elodie struck the wallpaper with her back, and Will pinned her there, his face twisted into a grotesque mask of red.

He felt her pulse hammering under his fingers, almost as loudly as his own. Perhaps he had overestimated her. Perhaps she was no better than all the other noblewomen. The bitter realization cooled his anger, and slowly, he forced it back under control.
“Don't,” he said quietly. He met her gaze in the mirror. “You will never defeat Mr. Arcos by surrendering to society's expectations.”

Like the evening after the scandal, when he had gone to his usual café and found that his friends had deserted him, leaving the table empty. “Is anyone else joining you?" the server had asked, but he had remained alone.

“Balto adores taxidermy. He skinned a vampire, stitched the hide back together, and filled it with reasonably fresh blood. The rest was simple enough—dress it and control the doll with a little blood magic…”
Unmoved, Mr. Arcos held the coat between them. “Then take off your shirt first.”
“Berserker may not have been the right word,” Mr. Arcos continued as Will peeled the shirt from his shoulders. Even beneath it, his skin was still sticky. “A fallen angel, perhaps…”

“No one leaves this city without sacrificing a great quantity of blood in a ritual, and most lose their minds before they can pay the price and turn a vampire. The real question, then, is why an interior designer?”
“I receive my tickets directly from the King because I travel in his name.” Slowly, he exhaled smoke into the night sky, veiling his searching eyes for a moment.
“There is no need to worry. You are one of us now.”
“Because I am not ready for the answer.” With that, he pushed open the door and was gone.
When he returned to the party and told Elodie he wished to leave, she did not object. But her gaze lingered on the coat, and something in it darkened. Something between them broke for good.

The full moon drew nearer, and every evening Hedgefort brought him a decanter of wine. Will followed Elodie's advice and drank himself into a stupor. No dreams came for him, though he could feel the moon swelling behind the curtains.

Together they made their way to the carriage while Hedgefort looked on the verge of a heart attack: Will in pearl white, like a fallen angel, and the duchess in red, like the demon tempting him from grace.

But it did not end there, though the dress alone would have caused more than enough scandal. No, she looked as though someone had flayed her: every inch of skin not covered by fabric had been painted scarlet, from her long red nails and slender fingers, up her arms to her swanlike neck and face.

“The full moon belongs to the vampires,” Elodie explained in the flickering light of the small oil lamp. “It strips the creatures of darkness of what little reason they have left. There is nothing but feeding and being fed upon. It is a dangerous night for ordinary citizens.”
“The Red Hand does, yes. He means to prevent blood mages from using the moon to perform major rituals without his permission. Everyone of rank and power is required to appear at his mansion.”

“No one is on your side. No one is on mine. We all fight alone here.” Elodie raised her pointed chin and turned away. He knew that some part of her wanted them to reconcile, but he also knew he was only a pawn on her chessboard.

Something struck the carriage without warning. The coach lurched, and Will clutched at the seat cushions while Elodie remained unmoved. Something scrambled across the roof above them, claws scraping and a hiss seeping through the walls. Then came a gunshot. A shadow tumbled from the carriage, and they raced on at a breakneck pace as though nothing had happened.

“I have a solution for the ballroom,” Will said at last, willing to take one step toward her. He needed to turn his thoughts away from the monsters surrounding them. “We break through into the floor above. The structure can support it—I did the calculations. And we make the floor marble so that it can be cleaned after a ritual.”
“Nothing a little magic couldn't solve.”

Up ahead, the Red Hand's gigantic mansion loomed—on an outcrop of rock in the violent surf before the cliffs, far too large and sinister. Even the lights shining far out across the sea could not drive away the darkness clinging to the place.

His body was immense, his chest rising heavily beneath a loose purple garment, while his pale face bore the traces of chronic pain carved deep into his expression. His thick arms rested on cushions as servants dabbed at open sores where his skin had split open. He looked like he was melting—his entire form, his skin, even his hairless head.

A young, half-naked woman lunged at him, stopped an arm's length away when the chain around her throat snapped taut. She strained against it with bared teeth and wild eyes, clawing through the air in an attempt to reach him.
“Your father recognized the potential in you from the moment you were born. And now you are one of the vultures circling my rotting body.”
“Eric has officially begun the contest for my succession. He killed two of your rivals—with his chimera, in full view of the entire Senate. Impressive.”
“I will kill you,” Elodie hissed so quietly that Will could barely hear. “I promised you then, and I will keep my word. But I will not merely destroy you. I will destroy everything you stand for.”
“Kneel.”
“No.” Elodie had regained her composure and fixed her uncle with a sharp look. “You will not have his blood.”
“He looks so obedient. But there is a brat in him. My favorite kind. Do you look this angry—” He paused, wheezing for breath. “—when you have a cock in your mouth?”
“Vampires are like humans with weak minds. If a mage drinks their blood, they obey. Keeping vampires as slaves is forbidden, but no one cares about the law when you are powerful enough.”
“No one—not even Mr. Arcos—makes you as angry as that man. And yet everyone is watching you with respect and fear now.”
“Tear open your veins!”
A group of laughing nobles watched him from the top of the stairs. One of them held a thin blade as long as her finger. She raised it to her lips and licked away the blood still clinging to it.

He passed through rooms where naked bodies met in a different dance, moving to the rhythm of their own music. He found places where pleasure and pain became one. Through a narrow door, he entered a room where a man hung in chains while people licked his wounds and sucked blood from his hard cock. Flickering lights, black walls. He stumbled into chambers where women sang, and statues spoke. He staggered through stairwells where guests sank into drugged stupors. He walked along passageways where the darkness lived. He touched walls that had a heartbeat.

Mr. Arcos held one hand above the dark body on the altar and, as the ritual came to its end, let his blood drip into the monster's mouth. Will recognized the red script suspended in the air and the swaying, chanting figures. A lifeless chimera lay before him.

Mr. Arcos stroked its leathery forehead as though it were one of his dogs, and the confused creature leaned into its master's touch. Everything about the gesture was so different from the terrible chaos of Elodie's ritual two weeks ago.
With a primal roar, it opened its jaws over the vampire's head, sank its teeth into the skull, and bit clean through. Mr. Arcos did not so much as blink. He merely stared darkly at Will.
“She's mad. She murdered her father.”
“Charles, isn't this your cousin?”

But none of it reached him. White noise roared in his ears, mercifully drowning out the sounds from the chamber. Yet the images remained before his mind's eye—pulsing, blinding, corrosive. He did not care that they were vampires. To him, it made no difference.

“No one in this city dies of old age. Sooner or later, we all end as vampires or fodder to them. That is the curse of this place. The only question is how long we endure before it catches up with us.”

“Under the law, vampires are considered dead. Killing one is therefore not a crime. Necrophilia is, however, and what you witnessed would lead to charges if it had not happened here, in the Red Hand's mansion.”

Perhaps. They can no longer tell us. Certain reflexes remain when someone succumbs to bloodlust, as do fragments of their personality. Those fade with time, and most lose every trace of reason. But you must never underestimate them.
Mr. Arcos pushed Will forward with one hand on his shoulder as though returning a runaway schoolboy. “Keep a closer eye on your pup before something happens to him.”

“When my mother learned from the Red Hand that a train ticket had been purchased, she insisted on buying one herself so that she could be the first to see who was honoring our city with a visit after so long.”
It is no wonder that the first thing you undertook after your father's death was a renovation." His pale eyes glittered with mischief. “You are growing into the perfect woman.”
The morning glowed pink as Will climbed into the carriage.

At last, panting, he pushed the sticky strands from his face. His hair fell in a silver curtain beside him as he let his head hang in exhaustion. White honey glistened on his fingers, while the taste of salt, sea, and fish clung to his tongue.
Bone-white, a monster peeled itself from the depths of the room, part bird, part wolf, part rotting carcass, gnawed down to bone and sinew. It was so large that it filled the entire chamber.

Suddenly, beneath the rushing of his own blood, he heard a second heartbeat pounding inside his chest. In panic, he grabbed at his stomach, smearing the pearlescent fluid across his skin, but he felt a flicker of relief when he found no swelling there.
“Who tried to take what belongs to me?” the god murmured.
“Ebb to my tide, calm to my storm, I will always come when you need me.” Almost lovingly, the tongue stroked over Will's face. Only now did he realize how cold it was.
“Part your lips for me, beloved. Take what I give you,” the Albatross whispered, and Will felt its attention settle upon his face. “Let me protect you.”
Will's eyes widened, his two hearts hammering loudly. Cold fear and shameful heat tightened around his throat, while reason screamed at him to flee. But he obeyed.
Then the tongue lowered into his mouth, sliding past his lips and forcing them wider. It thickened until Will's jaw cramped in the effort to take it all.

Eyes wide and fingers clawed into the sheets, he drank as the first pulse moved through the tongue. Once again, he tasted salt and sea. White honey ran down his throat as he swallowed around the tongue.
A surprising new contender is Duchess Ormonde, who has returned to society following her father's fall...

Duchess Elodie brings order to the harbor district. After Mr. Arcos drew attention last week with his successful vampire hunt—witnesses claim they saw him entirely unarmed (as previously reported)—the head of House Ormonde answered by killing two vampire pack leaders.
“We use them [vampires] like cattle—worse than cattle—and for that reason, they deserve at least the same protections as our farm animals.”
Earlier that evening, Ormonde reportedly read the ambassador's secret love letters aloud as midnight entertainment.
Elodie's dress hung in tatters, her wrists and throat bore the marks of restraints, and her hair was disheveled, leaves tangled in the curls.
“He thought it amusing to tie me to the gates of the Senate. I only just managed to free myself before the senators arrived.”
Perhaps I need more people like you in my life. With pure hearts and black souls.

When she did not pull away, he kissed her wrist, the torn skin and ragged edges of the wounds. His mother had kissed his injuries until they stopped hurting, but these made his head feel light and quickened his pulse. Warm, fresh blood stuck to his lips, and instinctively, he licked it away.
Her pupils were blown wide, devouring nearly the entire stormy sea of her irises. Her racing heart drove fresh blood into her wounds.
She left without a word, but her taste remained on his tongue.

“That you are a powerful mage Duchess Ormonde has claimed for herself. Supposedly, she is searching for a husband.” He phrased the last sentence like a question, then leaned across the counter with a crooked grin. “Has she noticed yet that you anchor in a different harbor?”

It unsettled him that the certainty he had felt ever since realizing the nude statues of male angels fascinated him more than those of women was wavering. That as a grown man who had long since embraced that truth about himself, he now dreamed of taking a duchess to bed.

Will had expected to feel more nervous, but now that he was here, a strange calm settled over him. He patiently watched Saint's sharp face and noticed the line of glittering earrings running along the curve of his ear. The redhead was beautiful in his own wild way, with freckle-kissed skin and an upturned nose.
But the list had come to him in a dream, whispered by a god who rode upon the long beams of the moon.

“Concentrate on your blood. Do you feel the heartbeat inside it? Take hold of it and keep it there. It does not have to become a perfect blade.”
“The bargain with the Albatross gave you magic and made you his Silver Hand. At twenty-seven, you will belong to him, body and soul. He is the only one who can free you from it.”
His lips crushed against Will's.
There was nothing romantic about the kiss—only desperation.
His soul was still trembling from the angel's voice, yet Eric's mouth against his, the weight upon his chest, began repairing the torn connections to reality.
“Not a word about what happened out there. I will deny everything.”
But how could getting what he longed for hurt so much?

Only a few months remained until his birthday, and the second heartbeat in his chest, once so familiar, had become a ticking time bomb. Yet his stupid, stupid mind did nothing but replay Eric's kiss and his cold rejection in an endless loop.

Instead of filling the pages with final sketches for the ballroom, he covered them with everything he could find about the powers of the Red Hand. About captive gods and the bargains they offered mortals.
Beige bandages flashed beneath the sleeves of her dress.
“He only wants your blood again so he can bring more ships into the city! Is there at least grain on them this time?”
“They never did anything that would have threatened my virginity, but give people the freedom to do whatever they want and eventually…” Elodie cleared her throat.
“Eventually, they forget their humanity. They hid it beneath lies like ‘research,’ ‘conditioning,’ and ‘necessity,’ but now I know they were only hiding from themselves.”
“But Wilkinson was one of those who was always there. The one who always saw me as a woman, never as a child. He loved it when they tied me to the bed, and my body tore itself apart in madness.”
“Perhaps I was once a victim, but they created a monster.”
“I do not believe that. The more you tell me about your plans and your past, the more convinced I am that you strike them down with righteous anger.”
“No. My father always treated him with respect. We will leave it that way.”
“You have to leave the city. You and Elodie—I have tickets for you.”
In the weak light of the hall, he noticed the thick silver streak running through Eric's hair, and the concern in his chest took on a new shape.
But instead of two moons framed in darkness, furious black abysses stared back at him.
There was only one explanation: Eric had attempted a ritual to obtain tickets for Elodie and Will and had paid the terrible price demanded by the curse—and had reached his limit.
“Run!” Eric's final word was barely understandable.
So this was where Elodie slept.
She had built herself a kingdom inside the library.
His blood had worked. The Albatross's promise had worked again and lifted the madness from Eric's mind.
“You. Will. You,” Eric growled. “Always. Since the moment I saw you on that damned train. Until then, my world—my promise—had been so simple.”
“Entirely me. I warned you about me. Warned you that only monsters dance here.”
“Do you think you will find a secret exit in here?” Eric laughed, seized his ankle, and yanked him back.
No. He did not want to run anymore.
“I have never done this before.”
“So naïve, little hellhound.”
“Did you turn your entire body into a beast?”
“Use your words, Ambassador. I saw it in your eyes. You know exactly what you want.”
“I have loved gods, but you…” Will managed, his fingers clawing into the rug.
“Because I do not regret it. What I did to you. That you cannot get away, that you are my prisoner. It excites me to see how completely I have made you mine.”
“How thoroughly you destroyed me.”
“It reminds me of my workshop,” he said, half to himself. Will had to strain to hear him. “This is how my chimeras begin. A pile of flesh and bones.”
“I sacrifice.”
“Eventually, you will run out of bones to sacrifice.”
“The angel told me that to become the Red Hand, you have to sacrifice the person you love most. If you stay and Elodie succeeds… the King will demand your life.”
“Are you really that blind? Do you still not see it? The only person in danger here is you.”
“So willing to sacrifice yourself.”
“Because this is how it was for me. You know this part of the story—my family lived in the mountains you traveled through by train.”
“After three days, I caught the god of the Hungry Pack and the Eternal Hunt, and he was amused by the child who had outwitted him, so he listened to my bargain: his power for his freedom.”

“Because he did not want more than that. He did not want to be bound to the fragile human body of a half-starved nine-year-old. He only made me more like him by giving me a splinter of himself. But he never made me a mage.”
“But your god never made you who you are; he is just using you to survive. So enjoy the power and remind your god that he is bound to a very fragile, but stubborn vessel.”
It was perfect.
“He declined weeks ago,” Elodie said with a shrug. “He cannot bear to watch me win.”
He had considered telling Elodie about yesterday, but in the end had decided against it. In less than twenty-four hours, he would be sitting aboard the train back to the Capitol.
His dark red suit hid them all.

“If I were marrying you, I would marry you in the silk dress,” he said before he could stop himself. He would never forget the sight of her wrapped in the soft silk, the storm in her eyes while the clouds broke beyond the windows.
“Then I suppose I shall have to become a widow soon.”
Carried by six vampires in chains, the Red Hand's palanquin divided the crowd like a ship cutting through a tide.
Hidden within the folds of her vast skirts, Will gently squeezed Elodie's hand. She returned the pressure, nearly breaking his fingers.
“You deserve this victory,” he added.
“We will see each other on the other side.”
Then she was gone, and Will watched four scarlet, disfigured priests enter the ballroom. Four months ago, the sight of them would have shocked him. Now, his thoughts remained with Elodie.
The hall had become a white fairy grove—a vast mosaic pond shimmered across the floor, and stone vines crept over windowsills and fireplaces.
“A blood moon!” someone cried, pointing into the red night beyond the windows.
“William Frank, a last miracle!”
“You stand accused of high treason!”
“I bear witness,” Eric said. “I saw it with my own eyes, but I wasn't able to stop him. He overpowered me, threw me to the ground, and freed the prisoner.”
“He even attempted to seduce my wife!”
“I have a train ticket that can take him back to the Capitol tonight. Let him become the Golden Queen's problem.”

For the first time that evening, Eric and Elodie's gazes met, and the tension of a midsummer storm crackled between them. Without a word, they fought with the twitch of an eyebrow, the lowering of one corner of a mouth. In a language they had perfected in childhood.
“I expect no gratitude,” he whispered and straightened again.
“Chain him inside the train, if he gives you trouble. I want him out of this city before sunrise.”
The Red Hand wanted him for himself. He meant to make Will one of his vampires.
Albatross. Hopelessly, he called the name into the emptiness of his heart.
What do you promise me? the Albatross asked, and suddenly Will felt the worm inside his belly.
You want love, don't you? You want my love. I will give it to you.
He was not certain what he was agreeing to. Whether from now on he would wake every night with a monster above him, somewhere between pleasure and captivity, somewhere between beauty and horror.
“Albatross!” Will screamed the name into the night.
“Catch me when I jump!”
Before he could say anything more, white light exploded from his chest.

As though a salt-laden wind had swept over them, crystals of ice and salt crawled across the bodies. They spread over the street like rays of sunlight, while frost flowers glittered across the windows around him and tiny snowflakes hung suspended in the air. Red moonlight fractured within them.
“You are mine, my pearl.”
Eric had been right. He should have run for the train. But at the same time, Eric had betrayed him in a last attempt to hurt Elodie.
Dark red moss, almost black, spread along the walls. It resembled wild-growing flesh or mold consuming the house.
Even if he found them, they would be dead. No one here was alive.
His head remained intact apart from a bullet hole in his forehead. But his body lay open, as though someone had slit apart a sack and spilled everything he had been across the people surrounding him.

The wall adjoining the small parlor he had intended to finish during the celebration appeared distorted. Long folds ran across the tracery he had shaped less than twenty-four hours ago, as though it were only fabric, a vast curtain someone had drawn aside.

Of course Elodie had succeeded. Whatever course the battle had taken, whoever among them had sacrificed all these people, Elodie had ended it with a bullet to the head. As though putting down a rabid animal.
In the Red Hand's castle, the walls had felt alive. Here, they truly were. Muscles, tendons, and veins stretched across every surface, leaving not a single inch bare.
With grim satisfaction, he lowered the candle. He might be in hell, but hell could feel pain.
Lids opened everywhere, covering the low vault like a grotesque sky of stars. And every one of them looked at him.
“Do you know which way I need to go?” he asked, but the eyes merely blinked.
A castle made of flesh and a body without skin. Black night pulsing with red veins. Eyes watching me everywhere, like stars across the heavens.
“And what sacrifice do you bring me, my child?” asked a voice older than this hell itself.
“My husband.” Elodie's voice was firm and unmistakable.
“Love is damnation. You damned yourself with this man, but not out of love.”
“You purchased a ticket for this young man with a blood toll—so that I would spare him?” the King asked, and Will shuddered.

She had wanted him present during her examination, knowing he would suffer with her and wish to protect her. When she invited him to Bloodgrove, she couldn’t have known that he was not interested in women.
“I'm here to be sacrificed,” Will said.
“I do not want to sacrifice him,” Eric interjected.
“Your uncle brought you to me as an infant, still wet with your mother's blood, your umbilical cord still attached.” The King smiled. “I ate it.”

With a muffled grunt of pain, the King tore one arm free from the wall and reached for his abdomen. Long, sharp fingernails dug into the flesh, and he ripped out a piece of muscle. “Eat, and become mine.”
With grim resolve, she bit down.
“You were never meant to be anyone's instrument. You were meant to be free.”
“We are all meant to be free, but I have to sacrifice myself so that everyone else can be.”
“But let Eric go. He is a good servant. Sacrificing him would be a waste.”
“You sacrifice your love, yet you do not ask me to save him. A true warrior. So be it.”
“You will not have what belongs to me!” The Albatross's voice thundered through the cavern, making the king recoil and sink back into the wall.
And in the next instant, Will's body reassembled—not as a man, but as a god.
Every blow he had struck against the King had also struck his friends.
“They say love is blind. And I was the fool who believed you would recognize me even blind.”
“You have one year. One year to free me from a curse that has imprisoned me for centuries. And if you fail, I will claim my sacrifice. You cannot flee far enough to escape my power.”
“One year. You must kill the Golden Queen to break the curse.”
A cloudy day dawned. Several tracks away, a white-and-gold train rolled into the station while commuters crowded across the platforms.
“Welcome to the Capitol.”
